_comment: Golden table for the stored-TOTP seed parser, which exists twice:
src/ts/totp.ts (parseTotpSeed, for the add/edit form, which has to split a
pasted otpauth:// URI as it is typed) and vault-core/src/totp.rs
(parse_seed, for the CLI, the desktop IPC command and the server).
tests/totp.test.ts pins the TypeScript side; envv-cli/tests/totp.rs pins the
Rust side against the identical cases. Reviewing two parsers for agreement
does not work — the same arrangement, and the same reason, as
Code GENERATION is deliberately not duplicated: there is one HMAC in this
project and it is the Rust one. The app asks for codes over IPC.
`parse` cases: input -> the normalised seed and its parameters, or null when
the input must be refused. `uri` cases go the other way: a stored seed plus
the entry's own provider/account, rendered back to an otpauth:// URI.

`params` is the third table: what an entry's four stored fields mean, read by vault_core::totp::Params::from_fields and by totpParamsOf in src/ts/totp.ts. It exists because those fields were read three different ways in Rust alone.

parse._why: A bare seed, as typed out of a grouped display. Spaces and case are normalised so one seed is one string with one fingerprint.
Padding and dashes are accepted: a user pasting an export should not have to know the difference.
A full URI: every parameter read, the label split, the account percent-decoded.
Omitted parameters mean the defaults, which is exactly what a bare seed means.
The issuer parameter beats the label half: the label is often years-old text a user typed into a phone.
A label with no colon is the account alone.
A percent-encoded space in both halves. Exports written by web tooling also use +.
Nonsense parameters fall back to the defaults rather than losing the seed. Half the URIs people paste are slightly wrong.
digits=11 exceeds what a 31-bit truncation can express; digits=5 is below RFC 4226's floor. Both fall back.
Lowercase scheme, lowercase secret, and the SHA-256 spelling that is not in the spec but is in real URIs.
Not base32. Storing it would give the entry a permanently blank code field with nothing saying why.
Base32 alphabet, but under one whole byte.
A URI carrying no secret= parameter.
otpauth://hotp/ is counter-based: it has no clock, so 'the current code' does not exist for it. Accepting it produces a card whose code never changes.

uri._why: The common case: a bare seed on an entry, exported to a new phone under the entry's own names.
The provider is vault data and therefore untrusted (invariant 4). Unescaped, this one would append a parameter of its own choosing.
No provider to fall back on: the label is the account alone and no issuer parameter is written.

params._why: Nothing stored. Absent means what an omitted otpauth:// parameter means, which is also what a bare base32 seed means.
Explicitly the defaults. Indistinguishable from absent on purpose — that is why the writers do not write them.
Nulls are absent. A vault written by a build that cleared a field rather than dropping it must not read differently.
SHA-256 with the dash real URIs contain.
Case is not meaningful in an otpauth:// parameter.
An algorithm this project has no HMAC for. Falling back beats refusing the whole entry over one field.
Ten digits is the ceiling and is kept: the truncated value is 31 bits, so an eleventh digit is a constant zero.
Zero digits would format an empty code.
The divergence this fixture was added for: 99 listed as a 99-digit credential by `envv totp ls` while `envv totp code` produced six.
Not an integer. JSON's as_u64 refuses it and Number.isInteger refuses it; both must land on the default rather than truncating to something plausible.
An hour is the ceiling and is kept.
A period of zero is a division by zero three frames inside a card renderer.
Negative values cannot round-trip through the unsigned field either.
One field wrong does not discard the other two.
